ai.literal: One's own flesh for increasing, he another's flesh who eats, how will possess compassion?
ai.translation: How can someone possess compassion if he eats the flesh of another creature just to fatten his own flesh?
ai.modern: தன் உடம்பை வளர்ப்பதற்காக மற்றொரு உயிரின் மாமிசத்தை உண்பவன் எப்படி இரக்க குணம் கொண்டவனாக இருக்க முடியும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet questions the fundamental possibility of compassion in a person who consumes meat. The word 'ūṉ' means flesh, and it is used twice to draw a sharp contrast between one's own body and the body of another creature. The poet asks how someone who eats another being's flesh merely to fatten his own can ever truly practice 'aruḷ', which means compassion or grace. The logic presented is that true compassion cannot coexist with the act of destroying another life for one's own physical growth.

ai.literal: Wealth possession to those who do not guard is not; compassion possession similarly is not to those who eat meat.
ai.translation: The possession of wealth is not for those who fail to guard it; similarly, the possession of compassion is not for those who eat meat.
ai.modern: பொருளைப் பாதுகாத்து வைக்காதவர்களுக்குச் செல்வம் சொந்தமாகாது; அதுபோலவே, மாமிசத்தை உண்பவர்களுக்கு அருளுடைமை சொந்தமாகாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet draws a direct parallel between material wealth and spiritual compassion. Just as wealth slips away from those who do not actively protect and cherish it, the quality of compassion cannot exist in those who consume the flesh of animals. The word 'ஆட்சி' (possession or rule) is used in both halves to emphasize that neither wealth nor grace can be truly held without the right actions. Eating meat is presented as fundamentally incompatible with possessing a compassionate heart.

ai.literal: Weapon held-they heart like, goodness inclines-not, of-one body taste ate-they mind.
ai.translation: Like the heart of those who wield deadly weapons, the mind of those who relish the flesh of another creature will not incline towards goodness.
ai.modern: ஆயுதம் ஏந்தியவர்களின் நெஞ்சம் எப்படி இரக்கமின்றி இருக்குமோ, அதே போல மற்றொரு உயிரின் உடலைச் சுவைத்து உண்டவர்களின் மனமும் நன்மையை நோக்கிச் செல்லாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares meat-eaters to people who wield weapons. Just as a person holding a weapon to kill lacks compassion, a person who eats the flesh of another creature loses their natural sense of pity. The word 'நன்' (goodness) here refers to compassion or grace, which cannot exist in a mind that enjoys eating another body.

ai.literal: Grace and that which is not, what are they, if asked: non-killing and killing; value, that which is not, is eating that flesh.
ai.translation: If asked what is grace and what is not, they are non-killing and killing. Eating that flesh is an act of no value.
ai.modern: அருள் என்பது எது, அருள் அல்லாதது எது என்று கேட்டால், அவை முறையே ஓர் உயிரைக் கொல்லாமையும் கொல்லுதலும் ஆகும். அப்படிப் பெற்ற ஊனை உண்பது அறம் அல்லாத செயலாகும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet defines grace and its opposite through the acts of non-killing and killing. It establishes that true compassion lies in not harming any life, while taking a life is the absence of compassion. Consequently, eating the flesh of a killed creature is condemned as an act devoid of any moral value or virtue. The word 'பொருள்' (poruḷ) here means a thing of value or virtue, emphasizing that eating meat brings no spiritual or moral worth.

ai.literal: Non-eating has the preservation of life; meat to eat, opening the mouth will not do hell.
ai.translation: The preservation of life lies in not eating meat. If one eats flesh, hell will swallow them and never open its mouth to let them out.
ai.modern: உயிர்கள் நிலைபெற்று வாழ்வது ஊன் உண்ணாமை என்னும் அறத்தில்தான் உள்ளது. ஒருவன் ஊனை உண்டால், அவனை விழுங்கிய நரகம் பின் அவனை வெளியே விடத் தன் வாயைத் திறக்காது.
ai.explanation: The couplet declares that the very preservation of life depends on the principle of not eating meat. The word 'uyirnilai' refers to the continued existence or standing of living beings. The second line uses a vivid image: if someone eats flesh, 'aḷaṟu' (hell) will swallow them and never 'aṇṇāttal' (open its mouth) to release them. This emphasizes the severe and irreversible consequence of consuming meat.

ai.literal: Eating for the sake of, does not kill the world if, anyone for the sake of price meat-providers there are not.
ai.translation: If the world does not kill animals for the sake of eating them, there will be no one offering meat for the sake of selling it.
ai.modern: மக்கள் உண்பதற்காக உயிர்களைக் கொல்ல மாட்டார்கள் என்றால், விலைக்கு விற்பதற்காக இறைச்சியைத் தருபவர் எவரும் இருக்க மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet addresses the argument that eating meat is acceptable if one does not do the killing oneself. The poet points out the direct economic link between the consumer and the butcher. If the world stops demanding meat for food, no one will kill animals to supply meat for a price. Thus, the eater is ultimately responsible for the killing, making abstinence from meat a moral necessity.

ai.translation: One must not eat meat, if one finds those who realize that it is but the wound of another creature.
ai.modern: புலால் என்பது வேறொரு உயிரின் புண் என்பதை உணர்ந்தவர்களைக் கேட்டால், அதனை உண்ணக்கூடாது என்றே சொல்வார்கள்.
ai.explanation: The couplet declares that meat is nothing but the wound or torn flesh of another living creature. The word 'புண்' (wound) starkly strips away the appeal of meat, revealing its violent origin. 'உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்' suggests that if one seeks the counsel of those who truly understand this reality, they will insist that one must abstain from eating it. Thus, true awareness naturally leads to the rejection of meat.

ai.literal: From flaw completely separated people of vision eat not from life completely separated flesh.
ai.translation: People of clear vision, who are completely separated from flaws, will not eat flesh that is separated from life.
ai.modern: குற்றங்களிலிருந்து முழுமையாக நீங்கிய தெளிவான அறிவை உடையவர்கள், உயிரிலிருந்து பிரிக்கப்பட்ட ஊனை உண்ண மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet draws a poetic and moral parallel between the purity of the eater and the nature of the food. The word 'ceyir' means a flaw or blemish; those who have separated themselves from such moral flaws possess clear vision and understanding. Just as these wise individuals are separated from faults, meat is simply flesh that has been separated from life. Recognizing this grim reality, people of flawless understanding will refuse to consume the dead flesh of another creature.

ai.literal: oblation having-poured thousand than-sacrificing of-one life having-destroyed not-eating is-good
ai.translation: Not destroying the life of a single creature to eat its flesh is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices.
ai.modern: நெய் போன்ற பொருள்களைத் தீயில் சொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேள்விகளைச் செய்வதை விட, ஓர் உயிரைக் கொன்று அதன் ஊனை உண்ணாமை மிகவும் நல்லது.
ai.explanation: The couplet compares the merit of performing grand religious rituals with the simple act of abstaining from meat. 'அவி' refers to the offerings like ghee poured into the sacrificial fire. 'வேட்டலின்' means 'than performing sacrifices', setting up a comparison. The text asserts that not killing even a single creature ('ஒன்றன் உயிர் செகுத்து') for food ('உண்ணாமை') is far superior ('நன்று') to conducting a thousand such sacrifices.

ai.literal: He who does not kill, flesh (acc.) him who has refused, having folded hands, all living beings will worship.
ai.translation: All living creatures will fold their hands and worship the one who never kills and refuses to eat meat.
ai.modern: ஓர் உயிரையும் கொல்லாதவனாகவும், புலால் உண்பதை மறுத்தவனாகவும் வாழ்பவனைக் கைகூப்பி எல்லா உயிர்களும் வணங்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme virtue of non-violence and abstaining from meat. It states that a person who neither kills nor consumes flesh earns the ultimate reverence of the natural world. All living creatures will instinctively recognize such a person's compassion and bow to them with folded hands. The act of folding hands signifies deep respect and gratitude from the animal kingdom towards their protector.
